_comment: Every stop worth considering. 'routes' lists which route options it sits on — a stop shows up only when one of its routes is selected. 'detour' is MINUTES ONE WAY off the highway; the app doubles it and adds 'dwell' to show what it really costs the day. 'first' flags something Ada has no California equivalent for. 'big' means it's worth rebuilding the day around. 'winter' is the late-Dec / early-Jan caveat and is the field most likely to be wrong — verify before committing to any of them.

stops.name: NASCAR Hall of Fame
stops.why: You're driving straight past it and it's better than it sounds — the banked track display alone shows you how steep 33 degrees actually is.

stops.name: Georgia Aquarium
stops.why: One of the largest in the world, with whale sharks — which exist in about four aquariums on earth.
stops.winter: Book a timed ticket; the holiday week is its busiest of the year.

stops.name: MLK National Historical Park
stops.why: His birth home, Ebenezer Baptist where he preached, and his tomb — all on two blocks, all free.
stops.winter: Birth home tours are first-come and limited; get there early.

stops.name: Legacy Museum & National Memorial for Peace and Justice
stops.why: Eight hundred hanging steel columns, one for every county where a lynching happened. The most powerful museum in the American South and it costs five dollars.
stops.winter: Closed Tuesdays. Give it three hours or don't start.

stops.name: USS Alabama Battleship
stops.why: A World War II battleship you walk through top to bottom, plus a submarine, four minutes off I-10.

stops.name: First look at the Gulf
stops.why: Warm, flat, pale green water and sand like sugar. Nothing about it resembles the Pacific she grew up on — and in December you'll have the beach to yourselves.
stops.winter: Too cold to swim, perfect to walk.

stops.name: The French Quarter
stops.why: Beignets at Café du Monde, brass bands on Royal Street, two hundred year old ironwork. There is nowhere else in the country that feels like this and it is worth an overnight, not a drive-through.
stops.winter: You'd be here right around New Year's — which is spectacular and also means book a room early and expect crowds.

stops.name: Oak Alley Plantation
stops.why: A quarter-mile corridor of 300-year-old live oaks, and an unflinching museum about the people who were enslaved there. Both halves matter.

stops.name: Space Center Houston
stops.why: The actual Apollo mission control room, restored to 1969 down to the ashtrays, and a complete Saturn V lying on its side in a building built around it.
stops.winter: Open through the holidays except Christmas Day. Very busy that week.

stops.name: The Alamo
stops.why: Smaller than everyone expects and right in the middle of downtown. Free, and it takes an hour.

stops.name: San Antonio River Walk
stops.why: A river one level below the street, lined with restaurants for miles. In December and early January the whole thing is strung with lights over the water and you take a boat through it.
stops.winter: The holiday lights run through early January — you would be passing at exactly the right moment. Verify the end date before counting on it.

stops.name: Natural Bridge Caverns
stops.why: The largest commercial cave in Texas, and 70°F underground no matter what the weather does.
stops.winter: Weather-proof. A good rainy-day answer.

stops.name: Balmorhea State Park
stops.why: A 1.3-acre spring-fed pool in the middle of nowhere, 72°F all year, with fish in it. Utterly surreal after four hours of West Texas.
stops.winter: Open in winter but check — it has closed for long repair stretches. Confirm before detouring.

stops.name: Marfa Lights Viewing Area
stops.why: Unexplained lights on the horizon that people have been arguing about since 1883. There's an official pull-out with a viewing platform. Might see nothing. That's part of it.
stops.winter: Needs full dark and a clear night. Only worth it if you're sleeping nearby anyway.

stops.name: Carlsbad Caverns
stops.why: You walk down into it through a hole in the desert and end up 750 feet underground in a room the size of six football fields. A big detour and one of the great places on the continent.
stops.winter: Fully weather-proof — 56°F underground always. The bat flights are summer only, so winter costs you nothing but the drive. Entry reservations required.

stops.name: White Sands National Park
stops.why: 275 square miles of pure white gypsum dunes. You buy a plastic saucer at the gift shop and sled down them. There is nothing like it anywhere else on earth and the detour off I-10 is worth every mile.
stops.winter: Open in winter and the light is best then. It closes for a few hours at a time for missile range tests — check the park's closure page the morning of.

stops.name: Scenic Drive Overlook
stops.why: One overlook, two countries, three states. El Paso and Ciudad Juárez spread out below as one continuous city split by a line.
stops.winter: Best at dusk when both sides light up.

stops.name: Tombstone
stops.why: The OK Corral, Boot Hill, and a main street that leans hard into it. Touristy in a way that's honestly fine.
stops.winter: Mild and pleasant in winter.

stops.name: Saguaro National Park
stops.why: Forests of cactus fifty feet tall and two hundred years old. The loop drive at sunset is the one.
stops.winter: Peak season — winter is the best time of year to be here.

stops.name: Pima Air & Space Museum
stops.why: Four hundred aircraft parked in the desert, including an SR-71 and a Boeing 787. Add the bus tour of the boneyard next door — 4,000 mothballed military planes in rows.
stops.winter: Boneyard tours are weekdays only and need advance booking.

stops.name: Desert Botanical Garden
stops.why: The best desert-plant collection anywhere, and in December they light the paths with thousands of luminarias after dark.
stops.winter: Las Noches de las Luminarias runs through early January and needs a timed ticket.

stops.name: Joshua Tree National Park
stops.why: The Cottonwood entrance is right on I-10, so this is a cheap detour on the last full day. Boulder piles and the trees themselves, which look invented.
stops.winter: Winter is the good season. Nights drop below freezing.

stops.name: Palm Springs Aerial Tramway
stops.why: Rotating cable car from the desert floor to 8,500 feet in ten minutes — from palm trees to pine snow. If you skipped Sandia, take this one.
stops.winter: There is usually snow at the top while it's 70°F at the bottom, which is the whole trick.

stops.name: Griffith Observatory
stops.why: Free, and the view of the whole basin at night is the last big thing before the drive turns into just getting home.
stops.winter: Closed Mondays. Parking is genuinely awful — go early or late.

stops.name: Salvation Mountain
stops.why: A hillside one man covered in half a million gallons of paint over thirty years. Strange, sincere, and completely unlike anything else.
stops.winter: Winter is the only tolerable time — it's 115°F here in summer.

stops.name: The Sixth Floor Museum
stops.why: The Texas School Book Depository, from the window itself. They preserved the corner exactly as it was found and the whole story is told from inside the room.
stops.winter: Open through the holidays except Christmas Day. Timed tickets.

stops.name: Fort Worth Stockyards
stops.why: A longhorn cattle drive down a brick street twice a day, every day, plus the honky-tonks around it. Cornier than Nashville and somehow better for it.

stops.name: Birmingham Civil Rights Institute
stops.why: Across the street from the 16th Street Baptist Church and Kelly Ingram Park, where the fire hoses were turned on children in 1963. The museum and those two blocks are one thing.
stops.winter: Closed Mondays.

stops.name: Vicksburg National Military Park
stops.why: A 16-mile drive through the siege lines above the Mississippi, plus a Union ironclad raised out of the river mud a century later.
stops.winter: Open year round, quiet in winter.

stops.name: Hoover Dam
stops.why: 726 feet of concrete wedged into Black Canyon in the middle of the Depression. You can walk out on the bypass bridge and look straight down the face of it for free.
stops.winter: Open year round and December is the pleasant time to be here. Security screening on the dam road.

stops.name: The Strip
stops.why: Whatever you think of it, there is nothing else like it, and walking it at night once is worth doing. The Bellagio fountains are free and run every half hour.
stops.winter: Cold at night in December — colder than people expect in a desert.

stops.name: Seven Magic Mountains
stops.why: Seven stacks of boulders painted in fluorescent colors standing alone in the desert south of Vegas. Ten minutes, free, and it photographs better than almost anything on the trip.

stops.name: Kelso Dunes, Mojave National Preserve
stops.why: Six hundred foot sand dunes that boom audibly when you slide down them. Almost nobody stops, which is most of the appeal.
stops.winter: Winter is the only comfortable season. Last few miles are graded dirt.

stops.name: Aji Amarillo
stops.why: A Peruvian counter operating inside a swap meet, huge portions for almost nothing. It is a stall, not a restaurant, and it keeps stall hours.
stops.winter: Closed Monday and done by 6:30. Hours run loose, call before counting on it.

stops.name: Pyrenees Cafe
stops.why: Boardinghouse cooking at long communal tables since 1901, the last Basque house in town that manages to open seven days. Three hours from home, so it only works if you left hungry.
stops.winter: Tuesday it closes at 3pm. Every other day it serves dinner.

stops.name: Tanger Outlets
stops.why: A full outlet mall right at the I-15 and I-40 split, the best shopping on the western half of the drive. Outlets always eat more time than you plan for.

stops.name: Peggy Sue's 50's Diner
stops.why: Full 1950s kitsch, chrome, jukebox, Elvis on the wall, and a dinosaur park out back. Seventeen thousand reviews, and the root beer float comes with a shot of extra root beer. The food is fine rather than good, you come for the room.

stops.name: Calico Ghost Town
stops.why: A silver town that died in 1907, bought whole by Walter Knott and rebuilt as itself. A good legs stretch a couple of hours in, if you can take the wind.
stops.winter: Open 9 to 5. Cold and very windy on the mesa in December.

stops.name: Seligman
stops.why: The town whose barber led the fight to save Route 66, and the model for Radiator Springs. It is two blocks, and the two blocks are worth it.

stops.name: Delgadillo's Snow Cap
stops.why: A 1953 drive-in where the family has been pranking customers for seventy years. Fake menus, doors to nowhere, mustard bottles that squirt string. The food is beside the point, the show comes free with lunch.
stops.winter: Winter hours are unreliable and they post closures on Facebook. Check before counting on lunch.

stops.name: Mr. D'z Route 66 Diner
stops.why: Turquoise and pink diner on the old road through Kingman, with house-made root beer in a frosted mug. Open 7am to 9pm every day. Come for the root beer and the room, not the cooking.

stops.name: Grand Canyon Caverns
stops.why: The largest dry cavern in the country. An elevator drops 210 feet into it, there is a hotel suite at the bottom, and it is 56 degrees inside no matter what the desert is doing.
stops.winter: Open all winter except Christmas Day, but off-season tour times vary. Call first.

stops.name: Oatman
stops.why: A mining town where descendants of abandoned pack burros walk down the main street and expect to be fed. Ada will remember this longer than most things on the list.
stops.winter: Come in from the Topock side. The Kingman approach over Sitgreaves Pass is 191 turns with no guardrails. Before 11am for parking, and bring cash.

stops.name: Historic downtown Flagstaff
stops.why: Compact brick downtown of bookstores, breweries and restaurants under the San Francisco Peaks. The best place to eat and stretch on the whole desert crossing, and an easy place to lose two hours.

stops.name: Puebla Sunrise Cafe
stops.why: Small family-run breakfast place downtown. Green chile omelettes, chorizo scrambles, and a reviewer who grew up in Mexico calls it the most authentic he has found in this country.
stops.winter: Breakfast and lunch only, 7am to 3pm. It has to shape your morning.

stops.name: Bearizona
stops.why: Drive-through wildlife park where wolves, bison and bears walk past the car. You never get out, which is exactly right in December.
stops.winter: The drive-through loop stays open in snow, and the animals are livelier in the cold.

stops.name: Walnut Canyon
stops.why: Cliff dwellings built into the limestone ledges of a narrow canyon, a short visit close to the interstate.
stops.winter: The Island Trail stair descent closes for ice. After a storm you may only get the rim. Trails close an hour before the 5pm gate.

stops.name: Sunset Crater & Wupatki
stops.why: A black cinder field from an eruption around 1085, and at the far end of the same road, red sandstone pueblos abandoned eight hundred years ago. Two completely different things on one loop road.
stops.winter: The loop ices and closes after snow, and it is a long way in to be turned around. Skip it in bad weather.

stops.name: Grand Canyon, South Rim
stops.why: A mile deep, eighteen miles across, and nothing on earth to compare it to. Snow on the rim makes it better, not worse.
stops.winter: Open all winter and plowed. The entrance road can close during a storm, check conditions at (928) 638-7496 before committing to the turn.

stops.name: Wigwam Motel
stops.why: Fifteen concrete teepees from 1950 with period cars parked outside each one. Nothing to do but look, and the look is worth the four minutes.

stops.name: Meteor Crater
stops.why: A hole nearly a mile across and 550 feet deep, punched by an iron asteroid about 50,000 years ago. The best astonishment per minute on the route.
stops.winter: Winter hours 8 to 5, and the rim is brutally windy. Bring the heavy coat in from the car.

stops.name: Petrified Forest & Painted Desert
stops.why: A national park you drive through rather than into. Fossil logs turned to solid quartz, badlands banded red and violet, and the 1920s Painted Desert Inn free on the rim. The park road runs alongside the interstate and puts you back on it, so most of the time is not a detour at all.
stops.winter: Gates run 8 to 5 in winter, closed Christmas Day, and opening can be delayed after snow. Morning or nothing.

stops.name: Earl's Family Restaurant
stops.why: Route 66 institution since 1947. Navajo tacos on frybread, huevos rancheros, green chile, and Navajo and Zuni artisans coming table to table selling jewelry straight from the maker. Half plates available, and you will want one.
stops.winter: Sunday it closes at 2pm.

stops.name: El Rancho Hotel
stops.why: Built in 1937 for the crews shooting Westerns here. A two-story log and balcony lobby hung with signed photos of everyone who stayed. Same exit as Earl's.

stops.name: Laguna Burger
stops.why: The original green chile cheeseburger counter, inside a gas station on old Route 66 at Laguna Pueblo. Hand-cut fries, open 6am to 8pm seven days. Seating is tight and the line can be long, it is worth both.

stops.name: Laguna Pueblo & San Jose Mission
stops.why: A brilliant white adobe mission church from 1699 above the pueblo, visible from the interstate. Same exit as the burger.
stops.winter: An active community with strict rules, and the church is often closed. If it is, look from outside and move on.

stops.name: Old Town Albuquerque
stops.why: An adobe plaza from 1706 around the San Felipe de Neri church. In the weeks before Christmas the walls and rooftops are lined with farolitos, candles in sand inside paper bags. Only works after dark.
stops.winter: The full farolito display is Christmas Eve itself. Earlier in the week the plaza is still lit for the season.

stops.name: Route 66 Auto Museum
stops.why: Restored hot rods and memorabilia attached to a working body shop, right off the interstate. Small, cheap, and open 7:30 to 5 every day.

stops.name: Blue Hole
stops.why: An 81-foot artesian spring in dry New Mexico, so clear you see the bottom from the rim. Divers train in it year round. You are looking, not swimming, and it is completely unexpected in that landscape.

stops.name: Tucumcari neon & Blue Swallow Motel
stops.why: The best surviving stretch of Route 66 neon anywhere, centered on a 1939 motel with individual garages. Tee Pee Curios and its 1944 sign are on the same strip. Dark falls by 5pm in December, so it is easy to catch lit.
stops.winter: The motel itself shuts for January and February. Mid-December the neon is still on.

stops.name: Mesalands Dinosaur Museum
stops.why: Bronze casts of real dinosaur skeletons, made in the college's own foundry, and you are allowed to touch them. Small, and the casts are beautiful.
stops.winter: Winter hours are Tuesday to Saturday, afternoons only.

stops.name: Buc-ee's
stops.why: A hundred-plus pumps, brisket chopped in front of you, a wall of jerky, and award-winning bathrooms. The best rest stop you will ever use. You will walk out having spent sixty dollars on snacks.

stops.name: Cadillac Ranch
stops.cost: Free, buy spray paint in town first
stops.why: Ten Cadillacs buried nose down in a wheat field at the angle of the Great Pyramid, layered in decades of spray paint. You are expected to add yours. This is the trip photo.
stops.winter: Deep mud after rain or snowmelt. Wear the boots, buy the paint before you get there.

stops.name: U-Drop Inn
stops.why: A 1936 art deco gas station in green and gold tile, the model for Ramone's in Cars. The exterior is the whole thing, and it is beautiful at night when the neon is on.

stops.name: Delvin's Restaurant
stops.why: Barbecue crossed with soul food. Ribs and brisket alongside twice-baked potato casserole and German chocolate cake, and the highest rated barbecue in Amarillo.
stops.winter: Closed Sunday and Monday. Closes 4pm Tuesday to Thursday, 6pm Friday and Saturday. Plan lunch, not dinner.

stops.name: GoldenLight Cafe & Cantina
stops.why: Route 66 burger dive open since 1946, the oldest continuously operating cafe on the Texas stretch. Green chile cheeseburgers, live music, about thirty seats, and reviewers who call it maybe the best burger ever.
stops.winter: Closed Sunday.

stops.name: Palo Duro Canyon
stops.why: The second largest canyon in the country, 800 feet deep and invisible until you reach the rim. You can drive to the floor.
stops.winter: Winter gates are 8 to 6 most nights, 8 to 8 Friday and Saturday. The descent is steep with tight switchbacks, do not take it iced. Day passes sell out, reserve online.

stops.name: Braum's
stops.why: Burger stand, ice cream shop and small grocery in one. They only build within about 300 miles of their own dairy, which is why you have never seen one. All across Oklahoma and the Panhandle, pick any of them.

stops.name: Edge Craft Barbecue
stops.why: Texas-style done by an actual pitmaster. Brisket sold lean or fatty by your choice, ribs with real bark, and the Texas Trinity platter is a pound of brisket, a pound of ribs and two sausages.
stops.winter: Thursday to Saturday only, 11 to 3, and they sell out. The line forms before the door opens.

stops.name: Naylamp
stops.why: Family-run Peruvian at family prices. Seco de carne, ceviche, lomo saltado, and the best food value in the middle third of the country. Open seven days.

stops.name: Bricktown
stops.why: A warehouse district rebuilt around a mile-long canal, with water taxis and restaurants. Walkable and a good place to eat and stretch, though it is built for evenings and you may pass at noon.

stops.name: National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum
stops.why: Western art, rodeo history and a full-scale frontier town indoors. Much better than the name suggests.
stops.winter: Sunday it opens at noon.

stops.name: Clinton Presidential Library
stops.why: The archive and museum on the Arkansas River, with a full-scale replica of the Oval Office. Riverside, well done, and completely weather-proof.
stops.winter: Sunday it opens at 1pm.

stops.name: Wright's Barbecue
stops.why: Cafeteria-line barbecue from an Arkansas competition family. Brisket, bacon burnt ends, deviled-egg potato salad, and a line that always exists but always moves.
stops.winter: Closed Sunday and Monday.

stops.name: Crossing the Mississippi
stops.why: The bridge itself. Half a continent drains through the water underneath you, and there is no river in California remotely like it.

stops.name: Bass Pro Pyramid
stops.why: A 32-story glass pyramid holding a cypress swamp, live alligators, a hotel, and the tallest free-standing elevator in the country. Technically a sporting goods store. Right off the bridge as you arrive.

stops.name: Gus's World Famous Fried Chicken
stops.why: Started in a tiny town outside Memphis and spread across the country on reputation alone. Thin, spicy, shatteringly crisp, and cheap. One of the great American fried chickens.

stops.name: Beale Street
stops.why: Three blocks of blues clubs and barbecue with live music out of every open door. If you do one night out heading east, this is it, and evenings are what the schedule is shortest on.

stops.name: Dyer's Burgers
stops.why: On Beale since 1912. The burgers are fried in grease strained and carried forward from the original batch for over a century. It moves by police escort when the restaurant relocates. A good burger with an unrepeatable story, plus an automatic 20 percent tip.

stops.name: National Civil Rights Museum
stops.why: Built around the Lorraine Motel, with Dr. King's room preserved as it was that day. Arguably the best museum on the entire trip. It needs three real hours or none, and it is heavy.
stops.winter: Closed Tuesdays.

stops.name: Limo Peruvian Eatery
stops.why: Chef-driven Peruvian in East Nashville. Ceviche trio, tuna tacos, picarones, and a reviewer's husband from Lima calling it the closest to real he has found here. Not cheap.
stops.winter: Closed Tuesday.

stops.name: Broadway
stops.why: Three blocks of honky-tonks with a live band in every one, from late morning until closing. The playing is genuinely good. Loud, touristy, and you may have already spent your evening in Memphis.

stops.name: Arnold's Country Kitchen
stops.why: The classic Nashville meat and three. Pick a meat and three vegetables off the steam line, cafeteria style. James Beard recognised, and locals fill it by five past eleven. The most genuinely Southern meal on this leg.
stops.winter: Weekdays 10:30 to 2:45, Saturday 11 to 3, closed Sunday. Lunch or never.

stops.name: The Parthenon
stops.why: A full-scale replica of the Athens Parthenon, complete, standing in a city park. Built for the 1897 exposition and never taken down. Odd rather than beautiful, and the scale is startling.

stops.name: Sunsphere & Market Square
stops.why: The gold glass ball from the 1982 World's Fair, with an observation deck, beside a walkable square. Quick, and a good stretch stop.

stops.name: Gatlinburg SkyBridge
stops.why: The longest pedestrian suspension bridge in North America, with glass floor panels mid-span and real views over the Smokies. Gatlinburg itself is a lot.
stops.winter: Closes for high wind. Check before driving in.

stops.name: Tanger Outlets
stops.why: The biggest shopping stop on the eastern half, on the approach to Pigeon Forge. Budget for the Pigeon Forge traffic on top of the time inside.

stops.name: Dollywood
stops.why: A full theme park in the foothills, and the Christmas run puts several million lights across the property. A genuine spectacle rather than a roadside stop, and a full day of the schedule.
stops.winter: Closed some weekdays in winter. Check the calendar for your exact day before promising it.

stops.name: HardWood BBQ
stops.why: Family-run with the smokers going out front and everything made in house, including the sauces. The highest rated food of any kind on this leg, and a 58-year-old reviewer called it the best barbecue he had eaten in his life.
stops.winter: Closed Sunday and Monday.

stops.name: Tennessee Aquarium
stops.why: Two riverfront buildings, one tracing a river from the mountains to the sea, one saltwater. One of the best aquariums in the country, right downtown.
stops.winter: Holiday week is its busiest.

stops.name: Black Mountain
stops.why: A small mountain town of craft shops and cafes east of Asheville, and it goes hard on Christmas. A gentle stop rather than another attraction.

stops.name: Downtown Asheville
stops.why: Compact art deco downtown of bookstores, breweries, buskers and some of the best food in the South. Very walkable, and an easy place to lose three hours.

stops.name: Cook Out
stops.why: Absurdly cheap trays and forty-plus real ice cream milkshakes, open late, all over North Carolina. You can feed two people properly for about fifteen dollars. Many locations are drive-thru only.

stops.name: Lexington Barbecue
stops.why: The defining Lexington-style house. Pork shoulder over hardwood coals, chopped or sliced, with red dip and red slaw, and the sandwich comes on a bun cut only partway so nothing falls out. Widely called the best barbecue in North Carolina.
stops.winter: Closed Sunday and Monday, and parking is tight. Worth its own outing once you land.

stops.name: Midwood Smokehouse
stops.why: Charlotte's best-known barbecue, pit-cooked over hickory and oak with all four regional styles on one menu. The burnt ends get named as the standout. Open daily.

stops.name: Saborcito Nica
stops.why: Nicaraguan food truck doing carne asada, nacatamales, tostones, quesillo. A regular writes that he has tried everyone in Charlotte selling carne asada and there is no comparison.
stops.winter: Opens 2:30pm and the hours run optimistic. Call before driving over.

stops.name: Discovery Place
stops.why: Hands-on science museum downtown with an aquarium and rainforest. Aimed at kids, and the best rainy day option in the city.

stops.name: Concord Mills
stops.why: One of the largest outlet malls in the Southeast, minutes from the Nicaraguan grocery, so the two make one efficient trip.
stops.winter: Holiday week crowds are brutal. Go early or go in January.

stops.name: Rinconcito Nica
stops.why: A Nicaraguan grocery, not a restaurant. Shelves of products from home, the drinks, the cheeses, the sweets, the actual brands, and the reviews are people saying it is the real thing, in Spanish. Open seven days, 9 to 8:30.
